concepts.explain: A reactive force field has no fixed list of bonds. It works out from the instantaneous distances how strongly each pair is bonded, and recomputes that every step -- so bonds form and break as a consequence of the dynamics rather than being declared in advance.

Every atom's partial charge is solved for at each step so the electronegativities balance. A charge stops being a fixed property of an atom type and becomes a property of where that atom currently sits.

One value per atom rather than one for the system. It cannot be printed in the thermodynamic output directly -- something has to reduce it first, by averaging it, or in this tutorial by building a histogram from it.

steps.title: Bonds that are allowed to break
steps.teach:
A block of amorphous silica, stretched until it tears.

Every tutorial so far has told LAMMPS which atoms are bonded and left it that way. Tutorial 2 made a point of it: a harmonic bond gets stronger the further you pull, so the nanotube could never break. This one uses **ReaxFF**, a reactive force field, where the bonding is worked out from the positions at every step -- so bonds break, form again, and the charges move around as they do.

Three scripts. `relax.lmp` equilibrates the structure, `deform.lmp` pulls it apart, `decorate.lmp` passivates the fractured surface with hydrogen. This first part is the relaxation.
steps.call_to_action: Read the four lines you were given, then press Next.

steps.title: Where the structure came from
steps.teach:
`silica.data` holds a small amorphous silica structure -- 192 silicons and 384 oxygens -- generated by an earlier simulation with a different force field.

It also carries the labelmap, which is why every command from here on can say `Si` and `O` rather than 1 and 2. Tutorial 3 introduced type labels in an include file; here they arrive with the data.
steps.predict: open `silica.data` and look at the Atoms section. Every silicon carries a charge of 1.1 and every oxygen -0.55. Under a reactive force field, will those numbers stay put?
steps.expect: No. Fixed per-type charges are what every force field in the previous tutorials used, and ReaxFF abandons them: each atom's charge is solved for at every step from its surroundings. The average silicon charge you are about to watch climbs from 1.1 to roughly 1.87 within the first few hundred steps, and atoms at defects end up far from either figure.
steps.call_to_action: Right-click silica.data in the editor and view it. Find the Atoms section.

acts.title: A force field with no topology

steps.title: Two masses
steps.teach: The data file describes the structure but not the species, so the masses are set here.

commands.explain: Silicon, by label rather than by type number.
And oxygen.
commands.hint: The mirror of the line above: the other label from the data file, and oxygen's atomic mass to three decimals.

steps.title: The reactive potential
steps.teach: Three lines, and they are the whole of the physics.
steps.predict: the parameter file is called `ffield.reax.CHOFe` -- carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, iron -- and you are about to map a type to silicon. Is that going to work?
steps.expect: It works, and the name is the trap. Open the file and the element table lists C, H, O, Fe, Cl, Si and Al: the name records what the parameterization was *for*, not everything the file contains. The element list on `pair_coeff` is matched against the table inside the file, so what matters is that Si is in there -- and whether the fit was ever meant to describe silica is a question the file name cannot answer for you.

commands.explain: ReaxFF computes a **bond order** for every nearby pair from their distance, and derives the bonded interactions from that rather than from a declared topology. Nothing in this script says which silicon is bonded to which oxygen, and nothing needs to.

notes.alternatives: `NULL` means use the defaults, which match van Duin's original standalone ReaxFF. A control file would let you set global parameters and output options.

notes.note: extra memory for the neighbor and bond lists
notes.alternatives: ReaxFF allocates its own buffers from an estimate, and a reactive system whose local density changes can overrun them. `safezone` and `mincap` buy headroom -- without them a run can end in a `bondchk` error or a segmentation fault rather than a clean message.

commands.explain:
Point at the parameter file and say which element each atom type is.

The two `*` wildcards are not optional decoration: a reactive potential is many-body, so one command has to cover every pair at once. The trailing list maps LAMMPS type 1 to Si and type 2 to O, in the order the elements appear in the file.

notes.alternatives: `CHOFe` names the elements it was fitted for -- carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, iron and silicon. Using a ReaxFF file outside the set of systems it was parameterized against is the commonest way to get confident nonsense out of it.

commands.text: fix myqeq all qeq/reaxff 1 0.0 10.0 1.0e-6 reaxff maxiter 400
commands.explain:
Solve for every atom's charge, every step.

This is what makes the charges in the data file a starting guess rather than a property. A silicon in the bulk and a silicon at a dangling-oxygen defect are different environments and end up with different charges, which is the measurement the rest of this script is built around.

notes.note: how often to equilibrate, in steps
notes.alternatives: Every step. Charges respond to positions, and positions change every step -- doing it less often means running with charges that belong to a configuration you have already left.
Loosening it makes each step cheaper and the charges noisier. `maxiter` caps the work when the solve is struggling, which happens when the structure is badly distorted.

steps.title: One number per species
steps.teach: The charges are the point of this tutorial, so they need to reach the thermodynamic output. A charge is a per-atom quantity, and the output takes one number at a time -- so it has to be averaged first.

commands.explain: One group per species.
And the other.
commands.hint: The mirror of the line above: the other group name and the other label.

commands.explain: The mean charge on a silicon: the group's total charge divided by how many atoms are in it. `charge()` and `count()` are group functions available inside an equal-style variable.
And for oxygen.

A different kind of variable: `atom` style, holding one value per atom rather than one for the system.

It cannot go in the thermodynamic output -- there is no single number to print. It exists to be fed to the histograms in a moment, which is the usual fate of a per-atom variable.

steps.title: Report them
steps.teach: Six columns: the usual four, and the two averages you just defined.
steps.predict: you defined `v_qSi` as an equal-style variable and `v_vq` as an atom-style one. Only one of them can go in `thermo_style`. Which, and why?
steps.expect: `v_qSi` -- an equal-style variable returns a single number, which is what a column is. `v_vq` holds one value per atom, so there is no single number to print; it has to be reduced first. The histograms in the next act are that reduction.

commands.explain: Every hundred steps.

commands.text: thermo_style custom step temp etotal press vol v_qSi v_qO
commands.explain: `vol` matters here as much as the charges: the barostat is about to resize the box, and the volume settling is what says the structure has relaxed.

steps.title: A picture where the color means something
steps.teach: Every earlier tutorial colored atoms by type, which tells you what you already knew. Here the color carries the measurement.
steps.predict: the color scale runs blue at -1, green at 0 and orange-red at +2, and bulk oxygen sits near -0.9 with bulk silicon near +1.8. Which atoms will come out green?
steps.expect: The ones that are neither: dangling oxygens with only one silicon neighbor, and under-coordinated silicons. In an amorphous network those are the defects, and they will light up green against a blue-and-orange background without anything in the script having gone looking for them.

commands.text:
dump viz all image 100 myimage-*.ppm q &
type shiny 0.1 box no 0.01 view 180 90 zoom 2.3 size 1200 500
commands.explain: The `q` immediately after the file name says: color by charge, not by type.

notes.alternatives: `type` gives the familiar per-species colors. Any per-atom quantity can go here, which makes `dump image` a diagnostic rather than only a picture.

commands.text:
dump_modify viz adiam Si 2.6 adiam O 2.3 backcolor white &
amap -1 2 ca 0.0 3 min royalblue 0 green max orangered
commands.explain:
`amap` is the color scale: charges from -1 to +2, blue at the bottom, green at zero, orange-red at the top.

The result is worth looking at properly. Bulk oxygen comes out blue at about -0.9, bulk silicon orange at about +1.8, and the atoms that are neither -- dangling oxygens at defects, under-coordinated silicons -- show up green in between. The defects find themselves.

steps.title: The whole distribution, not just its mean
steps.teach: An average charge hides the thing that matters. If half the silicons sit at 1.9 and a few at 1.4, the mean says nothing about the few -- and the few are the defects.

commands.text: fix myhis1 grpSi ave/histo 10 500 5000 -1.5 2.5 1000 v_vq file relax-Si.histo mode vector
commands.explain: Build a histogram of the per-atom charge over the silicon group: sample every 10 steps, average 500 samples, write every 5000 steps, into 1000 bins spanning -1.5 to 2.5.

notes.note: sample every N steps, average M samples, output every K
notes.alternatives: The same three-number pattern every `ave/*` fix takes. M times N must divide K, which is the constraint people trip over.

notes.note: treat the input as a vector of per-atom values
notes.alternatives: Without `mode vector` the fix would histogram a single global number, which for a per-atom variable is not what you want.

commands.text: fix myhis2 grpO ave/histo 10 500 5000 -1.5 2.5 1000 v_vq file relax-O.histo mode vector
commands.explain: And the same for oxygen.
commands.hint: The mirror of the line above: the next fix ID, the oxygen group, the oxygen output file, and everything else identical.

commands.text: fix myspec all reaxff/species 5 1 5 relax.species element Si O
commands.explain:
Ask ReaxFF what molecules currently exist. It walks the bond orders, finds connected clusters, and writes their formulas to a file.

This is only possible because the bonding is dynamic. In any earlier tutorial the answer would be whatever the topology said when the file was read.

steps.title: What is a molecule here?
steps.highlight: fix myspec all reaxff/species 5 1 5 relax.species element Si O
steps.teach: `relax.species` will list every distinct species and how many of each.
steps.predict: the block holds 192 silicon and 384 oxygen atoms. How many distinct species do you expect the file to report -- hundreds, a handful, or one?
steps.expect: One: `O384Si192`, the entire block counted as a single molecule. Silica is a covalent network, so everything is connected to everything. That is exactly why this file is worth writing -- once the structure is torn apart in the next script, the count stops being one, and O2 molecules appear in a column of their own.

steps.title: Let the box find its own shape
steps.teach: Give the atoms velocities and let a barostat settle the structure at room temperature and ambient pressure.

commands.explain: A Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at 300 K.

commands.text: fix mynpt all npt temp 300.0 300.0 100 aniso 1.0 1.0 1000
commands.explain: A thermostat at 300 K and a barostat at 1 atmosphere.

notes.note: let the three box dimensions change independently
notes.alternatives: `iso`, as Tutorial 3 used for water, rescales them together and keeps the box's proportions. A solid is not a liquid: it can carry different stresses along different axes, and forcing the box to stay in proportion would leave those stresses in it.

commands.explain: Half a femtosecond -- half what the previous tutorials used.

notes.alternatives: A reactive force field needs a shorter step than a conventional one. Bonds are forming and breaking, and the charge solve has to track configurations that change quickly; too long a step and the charges lag the positions they belong to.

commands.explain: Two and a half picoseconds. Short, but ReaxFF with a charge solve every step is far more expensive per step than anything so far -- expect this to take a few minutes.

steps.title: Relax
steps.teach: Watch `v_qSi` in the Charts window as it goes.
steps.predict: the data file started every silicon at 1.1. The charges are now free to equilibrate. Will the average silicon charge drift gently towards its new value, or get there quickly?
steps.expect: Quickly -- within the first few hundred steps it overshoots, drops back, and settles near 1.87, and the volume does something similar. Charge equilibration is solved to convergence at every step, so it is not relaxing at the pace of the atoms; it is already correct for wherever the atoms happen to be. What takes time is the structure, not the charges.

steps.title: Charge and volume, settling together
steps.teach:
`v_qSi` climbs from 1.1 and levels off near 1.87. `Volume` drops sharply, overshoots, and settles around 7.7 cubic nanometres.

The two are the same event seen twice. The structure came from a simulation with a different force field, so its bond lengths were wrong for this one; the box contracting and the charges rearranging are both the system finding out what ReaxFF thinks silica should look like.

This is worth remembering whenever a structure is carried between force fields. Nothing warns you that the geometry belongs to a different model -- you find out by watching it move.
steps.call_to_action: Compare v_qSi and Volume in the Charts window.

steps.title: The defects color themselves in
steps.teach:
Open the images. Most of the block is blue oxygen and orange silicon, and scattered through it are greenish atoms -- charges between the two bulk values.

Those are the defects: dangling oxygens, under-coordinated silicons, the places where the amorphous network did not close properly. Nothing in the script identified them. They emerged from the charge solve, because a charge is a statement about an atom's surroundings.
steps.call_to_action: Open the Slide Show or Image Viewer from the View menu.

steps.title: Write the relaxed structure out
steps.teach: The deformation script starts from this.

commands.explain: A text data file holding the relaxed structure and its equilibrated charges.

notes.note: leave the fixes' own sections out
notes.alternatives: Some fixes store per-atom state that `write_data` would otherwise append in extra sections -- here the species and histogram fixes. `nofix` keeps them out, so the file describes the system rather than the bookkeeping of the run that produced it.

steps.title: It is yours now
steps.teach:
Things worth trying before deforming it.

**Read the histograms.** `relax-Si.histo` and `relax-O.histo` are plain text and the GUI can plot them: **File** then **Plot Data File**. You should get two well-separated peaks, silicon near +1.8 and oxygen near -0.9, each with a tail towards zero. Those tails are the defects.

**Turn the charge equilibration off.** Comment out `fix myqeq` and re-run. The charges stay at their data-file values and the structure relaxes to something different -- which is a direct measure of how much of ReaxFF's behavior comes from the charges rather than the bond orders.

**Use `iso` instead of `aniso`.** Watch what happens to the pressure components. A solid held in proportion cannot relieve a shear stress.

When you are ready, `deform.lmp` stretches this block until it tears.
steps.call_to_action: Change something and run it again.
